summary: This informational RFC moves several outdated TCP extensions and related documents to Historic status because they were superseded, never widely used, or are no longer recommended. The affected documents are RFCs 675, 721, 761, 813, 816, 879, 896, 1078 and 6013. It updates RFC 7414.

eli5.summary: This is spring cleaning for old TCP rules. It marks the ones nobody should use anymore as historic so people don't follow them by mistake.

questions: what does historic status mean for an rfc
subtitle: A clean-up RFC that formally marks old TCP documents Historic or Informational so nobody mistakes them for current rules.

tldr.problem: Many RFCs about TCP piled up over the years. Some are superseded, some are no longer recommended, and some never saw wide use, yet the RFC database did not reflect that.
tldr.mechanism: This document changes the status of nine RFCs to Historic and eight more to Informational, with a short reason for each.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 675, 721, 761, 813, 816, 879, 896, 1078 and 6013 and updates RFC 7414, the TCP roadmap, whose conclusions it puts into effect.

today: RFC 7805 is an Informational RFC. It obsoletes RFC 675, 721, 761, 813, 816, 879, 896, 1078 and 6013 and updates RFC 7414; no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Clean-Up
sections.content:
TCP has a long history, and many RFCs describe its protocol, implementation and extensions. Some have been superseded, are no longer recommended, or never saw widespread use.

The TCP roadmap, RFC 7414, already reclassified a number of TCP extensions as Historic and gave the reasons, but it did not instruct the RFC Editor to change their status in the RFC database. This document does exactly that. It also reclassifies the other documents mentioned in the roadmap whose status was Unknown, moving them to either Historic or Informational.

For each RFC, a letter code shows its original status: S for Standards Track, E for Experimental, I for Informational, H for Historic, B for Best Current Practice and U for Unknown.
sections.eli5: An earlier list said which old rules were out of date, but nobody actually changed the labels on them. This document goes and changes the labels.

sections.title: Moved to Historic
sections.content:
Nine RFCs become Historic. All but one had Unknown status before.

  • RFC 675 and RFC 761 were replaced by the final TCP specification, RFC 793.
  • RFC 721 (out-of-band control signals) was a proposal not incorporated into RFC 793.
  • RFC 813, RFC 816, RFC 879 and RFC 896 were incorporated into RFC 1122, with some content also in RFC 5461, RFC 6691 and RFC 6633.
  • RFC 1078 (TCPMUX) should be deprecated. It changes connection establishment so that the three-way handshake completes even when a service is unavailable, forces all new connections onto a single port, complicates firewalls, and has very limited deployment.
  • RFC 6013 (TCP Cookie Transactions) is Experimental and should be deprecated. It uses experimental TCP option codepoints, which prohibit large-scale deployment, and alternatives such as RFC 7413 have more rough consensus and running code behind them.
sections.eli5: Some old rules were rewritten into newer ones, and some ideas never caught on. Those get stamped 'historic', meaning: read it for history, but don't build with it.

sections.title: Moved to Informational
sections.content:
Eight RFCs, all previously of Unknown status, become Informational rather than Historic. They remain useful as background or advice:

  • RFC 700, a field report on deploying a very early version of TCP.
  • RFC 794, which says operating systems need to manage limited resources, which may include TCP connection state.
  • RFC 814, guidance on tables and algorithms for tracking identifiers in a TCP/IP implementation.
  • RFC 817, general implementation suggestions.
  • RFC 872, which concludes the fear of using TCP on a local network is unfounded.
  • RFC 889, experiments with the TCP retransmission timeout calculation.
  • RFC 964, which points out specification bugs in the US Military's MIL-STD-1778, intended as a successor to RFC 793.
  • RFC 1071, implementation techniques for computing the Internet checksum.
sections.eli5: These old notes are not rules, just helpful stories and tips. So they get a 'good to know' label instead of 'out of date'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no new security considerations. Each RFC it lists attempts to address the security considerations of the specification it contains.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is being built, only labels are changing, so there is nothing new to worry about.
